extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, and publishers using The Chicago Manual of Style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying Chicago Manual of Style rules on spelling, hyphenation, names, and titles for copyediting and preparing text for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectival compounds hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectival compounds are hyphenated before a noun but not after a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noun forms are often left open; see related rules (old, mid, 7.87, 9.32) for exceptions and cross-references. Examples: 'a mid-eighteenth-century poet' (hyphenated before noun) vs 'her style was nineteenth century' (open after noun).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age terms (years-old) hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Age terms are hyphenated when used as an adjective before a noun and are open when used predicatively or as a phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a three-year-old' (hyphenated noun form), 'a 105-year-old woman' (hyphenated), 'a child who is three years old' (open), 'the debate is centuries old' (open). See also fractions in section 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds formed with cross-
rubrics_metrics.description: Many cross- compounds are listed in Webster's; if listed, follow that form. If not listed, leave noun forms open; hyphenate adjective, adverb, and verb forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a cross-reference', 'cross-referenced', 'cross-grained', 'cross-country'. If term not in Webster's, prefer open noun form and hyphenate other grammatical forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email/e- commerce hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated except for 'email' (now closed) and certain proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'e-book', 'e-commerce', 'eBay' (proper noun). 'Email' is a departure from previous editions and is closed. See also 8.154 for trademarks/brand names guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: President-elect and similar
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like president-elect, mayor-elect, county assessor elect are hyphenated unless the name of the office is an open compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the office name is an open compound, the hyphen may not be used. See entry for 'vice' and guidance on open compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: ever- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with ever- are usually hyphenated before a noun but not after a noun; some permanent compounds are closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ever-ready help' (hyphenated before a noun) vs 'he was ever eager' (open). Some compounds like 'everlasting' are permanently closed; consult Webster's.

rubrics_metrics.name: ex- prefix usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex- compounds are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an en dash if ex- precedes an open compound (see 6.80). Examples: 'ex-partner', 'ex-marine', 'ex-corporate executive'.

rubrics_metrics.name: -fold suffix hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: The -fold suffix is hyphenated when attached to hyphenated spelled-out numbers or with numerals; otherwise forms may be closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'hundredfold' or 'fourfold' (closed with spelled-out forms), 'twenty-five-fold' (hyphen with hyphenated spelled-out number), '150-fold' (with numerals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster + noun/adjective forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Noun forms with foster are open; adjective forms are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'foster mother' (open noun), 'foster-family background' (hyphenated adjective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with free (second element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds formed with 'free' as the second element are hyphenated both before and after a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'toll-free number' (compound hyphenated), 'the number is toll-free' (hyphenated after noun).

rubrics_metrics.name: full- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: full- compounds are hyphenated before a noun and open otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a penitentiary-like institution', 'full-length mirror' (hyphenated before noun), 'the mirror is full length' (open). Use -ful (as in cupful) in certain permanent compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postpositive adjectives (attorney general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postpositive adjectives like 'general' in 'attorney general' are always open; in plurals the adjective remains singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'attorney general', 'postmaster general', 'lieutenants general' (plural keeps general singular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand and great- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'grand-' are closed; those with 'great-' are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'grandfather' (closed), 'great-grandmother' (hyphenated).

rubrics_metrics.name: half- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective forms with half- are hyphenated both before and after the noun; noun and verb forms are open; some permanent compounds are closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'half-asleep' (adjective hyphenated), 'a half sister' (noun open), 'a half-hour session' (closed as permanent compound). Check Webster's for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: House compounds (house words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with house (e.g., schoolhouse, courthouse) are closed or open as listed in Webster's; if not listed, prefer open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'schoolhouse' (closed if in dictionary), 'safe house' (open if not in dictionary).

rubrics_metrics.name: In-law compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: All compounds with in-law are hyphenated; only the first element takes a plural form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'sister-in-law', 'parents-in-law' (pluralizes first element only).

rubrics_metrics.name: like- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: If closed in Webster's, keep closed; if not in Webster's, hyphenate; retain hyphen both before and after a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'childlike' (closed if in Webster's), 'bell-like' (hyphenated). Check dictionary listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: near- and -odd compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Noun forms with 'near' are open; adjective forms are hyphenated. Terms like 'hundred-odd' are always hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'in the near term' (open noun form), 'a near-term proposal' (hyphenated adjective), 'a hundred-odd manuscripts' (always hyphenated).

rubrics_metrics.name: on- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds beginning with on- are sometimes closed and sometimes hyphenated; check Webster's and hyphenate if the term is not listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'onstage', 'on-screen' (check dictionary), 'ongoing' (usually closed). See also 7.83.

rubrics_metrics.name: quasi- and pseudo- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Quasi-: noun forms usually open, adjective forms usually hyphenated; a few permanent compounds may be listed in Webster's. Pseudo- see section 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a quasi-public corporation' (quasi hyphenated as adjective), 'quasicrystal' (if listed as closed). Consult dictionary for listed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: self- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Both noun and adjective forms with self- are hyphenated, except where self is followed by a suffix or preceded by un-.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'self-restraint', 'self-realization', but 'selfless' (closed) and 'unselfconscious' (closed because preceded by un-).

rubrics_metrics.name: step- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with step- are normally closed except when combined with grand- or great-, where hyphenation is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'stepbrother' (closed), 'step-granddaughter' (hyphenated), 'step-great-granddaughter' (hyphenated).

rubrics_metrics.name: style- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective and adverb forms with style (e.g., family-style) are hyphenated; the noun form is usually open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'family-style' (adjective/adverb hyphenated), 'dined family style' (noun usually open).

rubrics_metrics.name: vice- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective forms with vice- are hyphenated before the noun; noun forms may be hyphenated or open—check dictionary or usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'vice-consul' (adjective hyphenated), 'vice president' (sometimes open; check Webster's and hyphenate if term not listed).

rubrics_metrics.name: web- and wide- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Website and related web compounds: noun form 'website' is open/closed as shown; adjective forms are hyphenated. 'wide' compounds: closed if listed in Webster's; if not, hyphenate; retain hyphen both before and after a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a website' (noun form open), 'web-related matters' (adjective hyphenated), 'worldwide' (closed if in Webster's), 'university-wide' (hyphenated, and retain hyphen in adjectival position).

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule for prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds formed with prefixes are normally closed (no hyphen) whether nouns, verbs, adjectives, or adverbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions when a hyphen should appear: (1) before a capitalized word or numeral (e.g., sub-Saharan, pre-1950); (2) before a compound term (e.g., non-self-sustaining, pre–Vietnam War; use an en dash before an open compound, see 6.80); (3) to separate repeated letters/syllables that might cause misreading (e.g., anti-intellectual, extra-alkaline, pro-life); (4) to separate repeated prefixes (sub-subentry); (5) when a prefix or combining form stands alone (e.g., over-and-underused, macro- and microeconomics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific prefix spellings and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Spellings for many common prefixes largely conform to Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary, with listed acceptable closed or hyphenated forms and noted exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples with exceptions included in the list: ante- (antebellum), anti- (antihypertensive but anti-inflammatory, anti-Hitlerian), bi-, bio-, cis- (cisgender but cis-Victorian), co- (coauthor but co-op), extra- (extramural but extra-administrative), hyper-, infra-, inter-, intra- (with noted intra-arterial exception), macro-, mega- (but mega-annoyance), meta- (meta-analysis exception), mid- (midcentury vs mid-July), multi- (multiauthor but multi-institutional), neo- (neo-Nazi exceptions), non-, over-, post- (post-World War II exceptions), pre- (pre-Columbian exceptions), pro-, proto-, pseudo- (pseudo-Tudor exception), re- (reedit but re-cover vs recover distinction), semi- (semiopaque but semi-invalid), sub-, super-, supranational vs supra-American, trans- (transgender but trans-American exception), ultra-, un- (un-English exception), under- (undercounted), etc. Consult dictionary for listed forms and capitalization conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics and quotation marks for titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago prefers italics for major or freestanding works (books, journals, movies, paintings, ships, species names, legal cases); quotation marks are usually for titles of subsections or parts of larger works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some titles (e.g., series names, websites under which multiple works appear) may be neither italicized nor quoted. For capitalization and punctuation of titles, see 8.156–201; for highlighting letters/words/phrases see 7.48–69.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal names: general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal names and initials of persons—real or fictitious—are capitalized; space initials; respect the preferred spellings of living persons where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary, Encyclopaedia Britannica, or reputable sources for spellings. Unconventional lowercase stylings (e.g., bell hooks) should generally be respected in appropriate contexts, though editors may avoid beginning a sentence with a lowercased name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names with particles (de, van, von, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalization and spacing of particles vary widely; consult authoritative biographical reference. When a surname is used alone, the particle is usually (but not always) retained and formatted as in the full name, and it is capitalized at the beginning of a sentence or note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Jean d’Alembert' (d’Alembert), 'Walter de la Mare' (de la Mare retained), 'W. E. B. DuBois' (DuBois usage noted). Check language-specific guidance in sections 8.8–8.16.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenated and extended names
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated last names or last names consisting of multiple elements should usually retain each element; if a person is generally known by a shorter form, that shorter form may be used after the full form is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For lesser-known persons without established usage, use only the last element (including particles). Examples: 'Victoria Sackville-West' (retain Sackville-West), 'Ralph Vaughan Williams' (Vaughan Williams).

rubrics_metrics.name: French personal-name particle usage
rubrics_metrics.description: In French names, particles de and d’ are lowercased (except at sentence start); when the last name is used alone, de is often dropped but sometimes retained by tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Jean d’Alembert' (d’Alembert), 'Charles de Gaulle' (de Gaulle retained by tradition). When 'de la' precedes a name, La is usually capitalized and retained when the last name is used alone (e.g., La Salle).

rubrics_metrics.name: German and Portuguese name particles in English contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Particles in German and Portuguese names are lowercased in the original languages and usually dropped when the surname is used alone; in English contexts, widely known alternative forms may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Alexander von Humboldt' often becomes 'Humboldt' when surname used alone; 'Agostinho da Silva' becomes 'Silva' in English contexts but 'Vasco da Gama' may be 'da Gama'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian and Dutch particle conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Italian particles are most often uppercased and retained when the last name is used alone; in Dutch names, particles (van, van den) are lowercased in full names but usually capitalized when the last name is used alone in English usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Gabriele D’Annunzio' -> 'D’Annunzio'; 'Johannes van Keulen' -> 'Van Keulen' when surname alone; 'Vincent van Gogh' -> 'Van Gogh'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish name conventions (two family names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish names often include both the father’s and mother’s family names; when the given name is omitted, persons are usually referred to by both family names but sometimes by one according to preference or established usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'José Ortega y Gasset' may be 'Ortega y Gasset' or 'Ortega'. For alphabetizing see section 16.84. Traditions about married women’s name changes are noted; consult usage or the person’s preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian and Hungarian name ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Russian names include patronymics and family names that can vary by gender; Hungarian names traditionally put the family name first but are inverted in English contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov' (Lenin) and his sister 'Maria Ilyinichna Ulyanova' (note patronymic differences). Hungarian 'Molnar Ferenc' becomes 'Ferenc Molnar' in English; treat initials carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and other Asian name guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Arabic surnames often include integral elements (Abu, Abd, Ibn, al/el) that usually should not be dropped; Chinese and Japanese family-name-first practice should be followed in English contexts for Chinese and Japanese names (unless anglicized); Korean names usually present family name first and are usually retained that way in English contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Abdul Aziz Ibn Saud' -> 'Ibn Saud'; 'Chiang Kai-shek' -> 'Chiang' (Wade-Giles), 'Li Bai' -> 'Li' (Pinyin). For persons known by anglicized forms, follow established usage (e.g., 'Akira Kurosawa' -> 'Kurosawa'). When in doubt, use full form or consult reputable sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and offices — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil, military, religious, and professional titles are capitalized when they immediately precede a personal name and are part of the name; they are normally lowercased when following the name or used in place of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'President Abraham Lincoln' (capitalized before name) vs 'Abraham Lincoln, president of the United States' (lowercased). Exceptions exist for promotional/ceremonial contexts and direct address. For abbreviations see sections 10.11–26.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles used in apposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When a title is used in apposition before a personal name—that is, as a descriptive phrase equivalent to the name and usually preceded by 'the' or a modifier—it is lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the empress Elisabeth of Austria' (lowercased empress) but 'Empress Elisabeth of Austria' (capitalized when treated as part of name). 'German chancellor Angela Merkel' (lowercased in apposition) vs 'Chancellor Merkel' (capitalized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil titles detailed guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil titles are capitalized only when part of the name; exceptions and varying practices in official literature exist. Use context-appropriate capitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the president', 'President Washington' (capitalized when used with name), 'the Washington administration'; for senator/representative examples see entries and 10.13 for abbreviations. 'Speaker' is often best capitalized in all contexts to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of sovereigns and rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Most titles of sovereigns and other rulers are lowercased when used alone; the form used with a name is capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'King Abdullah II' (capitalized with name) but 'the king of Jordan' (lowercased). Special historic and language-specific forms (e.g., Kaiser, Il Duce) have noted conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military and quasi-military titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Military titles follow the same pattern: capitalized when used as part of a person's name, lowercased in generic or following contexts; quasi-military organizational ranks follow the same rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'General Ulysses S. Grant' (capitalized with name), 'the general' (lowercased). For abbreviations used before names see 10.15. Quasi-military titles (chief of police, warden) treated similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious titles are treated similarly to civil and military titles: capitalized when used with a name, lowercased in generic usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Rabbi Avraham Yitzhak ha-Kohen Kuk' (capitalized with name), 'the rabbi' (lowercased). Some traditional forms such as 'the Dalai Lama' are treated specially (traditionally capitalized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate, organizational, and academic titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles in corporate and academic contexts generally follow the civil-title pattern: capitalized when part of the name, lowercased otherwise; named professorships and formal honorifics are capitalized as part of the full title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'President Robert J. Zimmer' (capitalized), 'the chief executive officer' (lowercased in general usage). Named chairs and professorships are capitalized when used in the full form; student-status terms are lowercased (freshman, sophomore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive titles and honors
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive titles (e.g., 'the historian William McNeill') should be lowercased and treated as apposition. Civic and academic honors following a name are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the historian William McNeill' (lowercased), 'Roberta Bondar, Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada' (capitalized honorific). For awards see 8.83 and abbreviations 10.22.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of nobility and honorifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of nobility are usually capitalized as integral parts of names; the generic element alone is lowercased. Honorifics and respectful forms of address are capitalized in any context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Prince Charles' (capitalized), but 'the prince' (lowercased). 'Sir Paul McCartney' (Sir is capitalized); 'the Honorable Angus Stanley King Jr.' and 'the Right Honourable Justin Trudeau' are capitalized as honorifics. For complex British peerage forms consult specialized references like Burke’s Peerage.
